_comment: The ideal closed-loop homestead OUTLINE (one person). Operator directives: 2026-07-05 'use Home as a page for outlining what we need in the perfect ideal 100% closed loop self-sustaining homestead'; same day: dual units 'metric (imperial)' so either background reads it instantly, plus TWO TIERS per loop: bare minimum vs a life of luxury with all the latest tech (assume comfort in space, not austerity). Every requirement carries tier: 'baseline' or 'luxury'. game_id is a REAL id in the game data (unit-test enforced) OR the empty string, which renders as a 'not in game yet' flag: the luxury tier doubles as the game-content gap list, exactly the operator's stated purpose. Rendered by BOTH the native Home page (src/gui/pages/homes.rs) and the web mirror (web/pages/home.html fetches /data/home_outline.json). Infinite-of-X: edit here, both surfaces update. Top-level data/ so the web deploy publishes it. No em dashes in copy (operator rule). RE-AUDITED 2026-07-31 (second balance pass, checking the 2026-07-30 pass's own arithmetic). Eleven numbers in the previous pass did not survive re-derivation, including a factor-of-ten slip in rain catchment, a heating calculation that credited free gains twice, a luxury power figure that was impossible in two directions at once, and a nutrient balance that never counted the food the farm actually grows. All are corrected below and each correction names what it replaced. TWO loops are now flagged closes:false: nutrients (phosphorus, unchanged verdict, sharper numbers) and air (the SEALED case does not close at the bare-minimum power tier, a new finding). Per-loop fields 'balance' and 'assumptions', the top-level 'assumptions', and the new top-level 'scaling' carry the arithmetic; NEITHER RENDERER READS THEM YET (see in_game_next).
title: The ideal closed-loop homestead
subtitle: One person, seven loops, two tiers: the bare minimum that keeps you alive, and a life of luxury with all the latest tech. Both honestly sized, in metric and imperial, for a named place.
intro: 100% closure is physically impossible (entropy always leaks), but a single person CAN close energy, water, climate, and food, and air too as long as they are standing on Earth. Every number below is a balance: what goes out per person per day against what comes back, with the assumption set beside it, because an unstated assumption makes a balance unfalsifiable. Where a loop does not close, it says so and states the size of the residual. Two do not. Nutrients does not close because nothing on a homestead makes phosphorus. Air does not close in a SEALED habitat at the bare-minimum power budget, because regenerating one person's oxygen costs more electricity than the entire bare-minimum home draws. What one home cannot close is listed last, on purpose: those gaps are why community and trade exist.
assumptions: PLACE: Silverdale, WA, USA, about 47.6 N, the site already named in data/self_sufficiency/location.ron. Everything below is sized for open Earth at that site unless a loop calls out the sealed mothership case separately. Move the homestead and most of these numbers move with it.

SUN: NREL NSRDB / PVWatts for Puget Sound gives 3.9 peak sun hours per day annual average (regional range 3.5 to 4.2), about 6.0 in June and about 1.3 to 1.5 in December. An off-grid array is sized for December, never for the annual average.

PV DERATE: 0.75 end to end, being 0.86 (PVWatts default system losses) x 0.96 (inverter) x 0.91 (battery round trip), because in an off-grid home most energy is time shifted through the battery. The older 0.80 figure omitted the battery round trip.
OCCUPANT: one adult, moderately active (FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 Human Energy Requirements, physical activity level 1.75), which is what homestead labour actually is.

CLIMATE: 2,610 heating degree days base 18.3 C (68 F) and 44 cooling degree days, both in Celsius days. Note that location.ron records 4,700 HDD against a stated 18.3 C base; 4,700 is the Fahrenheit day figure base 65 F, so the file mixes conventions. 4,700 F days divided by 1.8 is the 2,610 C days used here.

DEGREE DAY METHOD (corrected 2026-07-31): heating degree days at base 18.3 C ALREADY credit about 1.7 K of free internal and solar gains, which is why the base sits below a 20 C setpoint. Multiplying a heat loss coefficient by HDD(18.3) and THEN subtracting the full internal gains counts those gains twice, which is what the 2026-07-30 pass did. Every heating figure below uses the balance point method instead: net heat = heat loss coefficient x HDD(base = 20 C minus gains divided by the heat loss coefficient).

SHELL: the ten room house of docs/design/homestead.md section 3, 16 x 20 m (52 x 66 ft) on one storey with 3 m (10 ft) ceilings, high performance envelope: walls U 0.15, roof U 0.10, floor U 0.15, triple glazing U 0.80 W/m2K, heat recovery ventilation at 85%.

CROPPING: sun lit greenhouse, no supplemental lighting, so November to February is a light famine that storage covers rather than production. Outdoor field is dry farmed, which is standard practice here because the growing season IS the dry season.

DIET SPLIT, stated because every area below is derived from it: 2,600 kcal/day eaten as grain 1,200, pulse 700, greenhouse vegetables and roots and oilseed and mushroom 550, fish 150. Harvest must exceed intake by about 15% for seed and storage losses, so the harvest target is about 3,000 kcal/day.

The five open loops in data/self_sufficiency/cannot_close.ron stay open. Nothing in this audit closed any of them, and the corrected nutrients numbers make the raw chemistry entry stronger, not weaker.

loops.name: Power
loops.demand: Bare minimum: the itemised list is air recycler 0.60, aquaponic air pump 1.20, cooking 0.60, cold storage and chargers 0.70, tower pumps 0.27, lighting 0.20, water pump plus purifier plus irrigation 0.19, which SUMS TO 3.76 kWh/day. The design target is 4.0 kWh/day, so 0.24 kWh/day is unallocated margin, and that is now stated rather than hidden in a rounded headline. Hot water sits on the biomass stove and there is no washing machine. A life of luxury runs 16.0 kWh/day: the 4.0 baseline plus climate 5.0, hot water on demand 2.0, fridge and freezer 1.5, washer and dryer 1.0, computers and entertainment 1.5, kitchen appliances 0.3, 3D printer 0.2, power tools 0.5. Peak draw is a separate problem from energy: about 3.9 kW at bare minimum (a 2.4 kW oven plus a kettle) and about 7 kW at luxury.
loops.closure_note: Sized for DECEMBER, because that is the month that decides an off-grid array. One 400 W panel at this site yields 1.17 kWh/day annual average and 0.39 kWh/day in December (0.4 kW x 1.3 sun hours x 0.75 derate). Bare minimum needs 4.0 divided by 0.39, which is 10.3, so 11 panels: 4.29 kWh/day in December plus 0.7 kWh/day of wind, a 25 percent margin in the worst month and a 3.4x surplus in summer that you simply dump. CORRECTED FROM 4 PANELS: the old figure assumed 4.5 sun hours and named no location; at the site this design actually names, 4 panels deliver 1.56 kWh/day in December against a 4.0 kWh/day load, a 43 percent shortfall held for about 90 days, roughly 157 kWh per winter that no 8 kWh battery can carry. Storage is sized to a 5 day overcast stretch at 0.4 sun hours, which is a 9.9 kWh hole, so 3 banks and 12 kWh rather than 2 and 8. Luxury keeps deep winter on the biomass stove, so its December electrical load is 11.0 kWh/day, needing 28 panels and 9 banks. CORRECTED THIS PASS, three numbers. First, the all electric December fork: the previous pass said 23.8 kWh/day would need 39 panels, and that is impossible in both directions, because the load is 11.0 base plus 20.0 for the heat pump equals 31.0 kWh/day, and 39 panels only make 15.9 kWh/day in December anyway. The honest figure is 78 panels, a 31 kW array, to heat this house electrically through a Puget Sound December. Second, luxury storage: the 5 day overcast hole at comfort draw is 34.7 kWh, so 9 banks is the floor and 10 gives 15 percent margin; the previous pass said 8 banks fell 6 kWh short, when they fall 2.7 kWh short. Third, the biodigester: 0.37 kWh/day is 135 kWh a year against a 1,460 kWh annual baseline load, which is 9 percent not 7, and it buys about 1.3 hours of generator run a week, not 2. The claim that the biodigester brews the winter generator's fuel remains over stated by roughly 3x; the rest of that fuel is traded.
balance: Demand, itemised: 0.60 + 1.20 + 0.60 + 0.70 + 0.27 + 0.20 + 0.19 = 3.76 kWh/day. Design target 4.00, so 0.24 kWh/day is stated margin, not a rounding artefact.
Supply per panel: 0.400 kW x 3.9 sun-h x 0.75 = 1.17 kWh/day annual; 0.400 kW x 1.3 sun-h x 0.75 = 0.39 kWh/day December.
Baseline December: 11 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 wind = 4.99 kWh/day vs 4.00 kWh/day demand. Margin +0.99 kWh/day (+25%). CLOSES.
Baseline annual: 11 x 1.17 + 0.7 = 13.6 kWh/day vs 4.0. Surplus 9.6 kWh/day, unavoidable when the array is winter sized.
Old spec check: 4 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 = 2.26 kWh/day December vs 4.00. DEFICIT 1.74 kWh/day for about 90 days = 157 kWh/winter.
Storage: 5 day overcast at 0.4 sun-h gives 11 x 0.12 + 0.7 = 2.02 kWh/day, deficit 1.98 x 5 = 9.9 kWh. 3 banks = 12 kWh usable. CLOSES.
Luxury December, deep winter heat on biomass: 11.0 kWh/day demand, (11.0 - 0.7) / 0.39 = 26.4, so 28 panels x 0.39 + 0.7 = 11.6 kWh/day. Margin +5.6%. CLOSES.

Luxury storage, CORRECTED: 5 day overcast at 28 panels = 28 x 0.12 + 0.7 = 4.06 kWh/day vs 11.0 demand, deficit 6.94 x 5 = 34.7 kWh. 9 banks = 36 kWh is the floor; 10 banks = 40 kWh gives 15% margin. The previous pass said 8 banks were 6 kWh short; 8 banks = 32 kWh and are 2.7 kWh short.

Luxury all electric December, CORRECTED: 11.0 base + 20.0 heat pump (see the climate loop) = 31.0 kWh/day. Panels = (31.0 - 0.7) / 0.39 = 77.7, so 78 panels, a 31 kW array, on a house that draws 16 kWh/day averaged. DOES NOT CLOSE at any sane array; this is the fork the previous pass mis-stated as 23.8 kWh/day and 39 panels.

Biogas, CORRECTED: 1.5 kg/day feedstock x ~0.17 m3/kg = 0.25 m3 biogas at 60% CH4 = 0.15 m3 CH4 x 35.8 MJ/m3 = 5.4 MJ = 1.5 kWh thermal x 0.25 genset efficiency = 0.37 kWh/day electric = 135 kWh/year against a 1,460 kWh/year baseline load, which is 9%, not the 7% previously stated. At 2 kW that is 2.6 kWh/week, about 1.3 hours of generator run, not 2.
Peak vs average: battery banks discharge 2 kW each, so 3 banks = 6 kW and a 2.4 kW oven is 40% of the bus. The old 2 bank spec gave 4 kW and the oven alone was 60% of it.

Sealed habitat cross-reference: add the air loop's 5.8 kWh/day of life support and the bare minimum becomes 9.8 kWh/day, needing 24 panels and 8 banks. See the air loop, which is why it is now flagged as not closing at this tier.
assumptions: NREL NSRDB Puget Sound: 3.9 peak sun hours annual, 6.0 June, 1.3 December.
Derate 0.75 = 0.86 PVWatts losses x 0.96 inverter x 0.91 battery round trip.
battery_bank capacity 4 kWh usable per bank, 2 kW charge and discharge (data/machines/home_solo.ron).
Biogas yield 0.15 to 0.25 m3 per kg of wet mixed food waste and humanure, methane fraction 0.55 to 0.65, small genset electrical efficiency 0.20 to 0.28.

Appliance draws are the per unit figures already in data/machines/home_solo.ron; note that since the v0.1027 plumbing increment that file also places a 1.2 kWh/day water heater and a 0.3 kWh/day washer that the 4.0 kWh/day baseline explicitly does NOT include, because at bare minimum hot water is on the stove and laundry is by hand.

loops.name: Water
loops.demand: Bare minimum 85 L/day (22 gal/day) net household, which is the actual fixture list and not a round number: drinking and cooking 5, kitchen sink 15, bathroom sink 5, shower 35, toilet 14, laundry 11. Luxury about 120 L/day (32 gal/day) with long hot showers, more laundry, and a dishwasher. Irrigation is a real and much larger flow: about 400 L/day (106 gal/day) of evapotranspiration off the 200 m2 greenhouse canopy in the growing season, peaking near 640 L/day (169 gal/day) in July, and it is NOT covered by greywater alone.
loops.closure_note: CORRECTED TWICE, and the second correction was a factor of ten. The 2026-07-30 pass rightly killed the old claim of 155 L/day of greywater recovery against an 80 L/day household, which was 194 percent recovery and physically impossible (it was the three person home.ron number imported without scaling); one person's greywater producing fixtures are kitchen sink, bathroom sink, shower, and laundry, totalling 66 L/day (17 gal/day), which at 90 percent recovery is 59 L/day (16 gal/day), a possible 69 percent. But that same pass then said the driest 90 days deliver 2,040 L of rain catchment, or 23 L/day. Redo it: 75 mm of rain on 320 m2 of roof at a 0.85 runoff coefficient is 0.075 x 320 x 0.85 = 20.4 m3, which is 20,400 L, or 227 L/day. The published figure was low by exactly 10x, and the consequence is that the dry season story inverts. Rain alone covers the 85 L/day household 2.7 times over even in the driest quarter of a Puget Sound year, and the 5,610 L cistern drawdown the previous pass used to justify an 8,000 L tank does not exist. What actually sizes the cistern is the longest genuinely rainless RUN, which here is 40 to 50 days in July and August: at a net draw of 86 L/day that is 3,870 L (1,020 gal) against an 8,000 L (2,100 gal) tank, so it closes with 52 percent of the tank still unused. The evapotranspiration term the original outline omitted entirely is real and is now sized to the greenhouse the food loop actually derives, 200 m2 rather than an asserted 350: at a Puget Sound growing season reference ET0 of 2.8 mm/day and an under glass factor of 0.70 that is 2.0 mm/day, so 400 L/day. Recovering 85 percent of it as condensate, the same closure BIOS-3 measured, leaves 60 L/day of net irrigation, which the 59 L/day of greywater covers almost exactly. Without condensate recovery the greenhouse needs 400 L/day of real water and the well, not the cistern, is what carries it: 426 L/day of net draw is 3.5 hours a day of pumping at 2 L/min. The outdoor field is dry farmed, which is normal practice here, and that is also the honest reason the pulse crop is the weak one (see the food loop).
balance: Household in: 85 L/day baseline, 120 L/day luxury.
Greywater out: kitchen 15 + bath sink 5 + shower 35 + laundry 11 = 66 L/day; x 0.90 recovery = 59 L/day. Recovery ratio 59/85 = 69%, which is physically possible. The pre-audit 155/80 = 194% was not.
Rain catchment, annual: 1.400 m x 320 m2 x 0.85 = 381 m3/year = 1,044 L/day average.
Rain catchment, driest 90 days, CORRECTED: 0.075 m x 320 m2 x 0.85 = 20.4 m3 = 20,400 L = 227 L/day. The 2026-07-30 figure of 2,040 L and 23 L/day was low by a factor of 10.

Dry quarter balance: net draw 85 household + 60 net irrigation - 59 greywater = 86 L/day, so 7,740 L over 90 days against 20,400 L caught. SURPLUS 12,660 L. The cistern never empties in an average dry season.
What actually sizes the cistern: the longest rainless run, 40 to 50 days. 86 L/day x 45 = 3,870 L against an 8,000 L tank. Margin 4,130 L (52%). CLOSES.
Same run without condensate recovery: 85 + 400 - 59 = 426 L/day x 45 = 19,170 L, which no 8,000 L cistern holds. The well carries it: 426 L/day at 2 L/min is 3.5 h/day of pumping.
Autonomy on the cistern alone: 8,000 / 85 = 94 days baseline; 8,000 / 120 = 67 days luxury.

Greenhouse evapotranspiration, resized to the derived canopy: FAO-56 reference ET0 about 2.8 mm/day growing season average outdoors (range 2.5 to 3.0), x 0.70 under glass including the crop coefficient = 2.0 mm/day; 200 m2 x 2.0 = 400 L/day, peaking about 640 L/day in July at ET0 4.5.
Condensate recovery at 85% leaves 400 x 0.15 = 60 L/day net, and greywater is 59 L/day. The two match to within 2%, which is the whole reason the irrigation loop is affordable.
Well backstop: 2.0 L/min = 2,880 L/day when run, so it refills a day's household use in 30 minutes and a day's gross irrigation in 3.5 hours.

DATA CONTRADICTION FOUND: data/machines/home.ron gives water_pump a display stat of 12 L/min while its own Water OUT port carries flow_lpm 2.0, a 6x disagreement inside one machine definition. The 2.0 L/min port figure is the one used above and the one data/self_sufficiency/component_outputs.ron cites.
assumptions: Fixture flows are the per person figures already in data/machines/home_solo.ron as of v0.1027.

Runoff coefficient 0.85 for a metal or membrane roof; 1,400 mm annual rainfall from data/self_sufficiency/location.ron, of which about 75% falls October to April and July plus August together are only about 50 mm.

Driest 90 day window taken as 75 mm, mid June to mid September, consistent with location.ron's own July and August note; the longest genuinely rainless run taken as 45 days, which is normal for a Puget Sound summer.

FAO-56 Penman Monteith reference ET0 for the Puget Sound growing season 2.5 to 3.0 mm/day (WSU irrigation water requirement magnitude for western Washington), point 2.8, July peak about 4.5; greenhouse factor 0.70 bundles the reduction in radiation and wind under glass with a full canopy crop coefficient.

Condensate recovery 85%, the mid of the 80 to 95% range closed greenhouses and BIOS-3 achieved. This requires a genuinely closed greenhouse; a vented one recovers nothing and the well carries irrigation instead.

requirements.why: 8,000 L (2,100 gal); the 45 day rainless run draws 3,870 L (1,020 gal), so it closes with half the tank spare and 94 days of household autonomy
320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) of roof at 0.85 runoff; 1,044 L/day annual average and still 227 L/day through the driest 90 days, which is 2.7x the household need
2 L/min (0.5 gal/min); 30 minutes covers a day of household use, 3.5 hours covers a day of gross greenhouse irrigation
240 L/day (63 gal/day) potable polish, 2.8x the one person need
the six fixtures that sum to the real 85 L/day: cistern to pump to purifier to taps
recovers 59 L/day (16 gal/day) from sinks, shower, and laundry, which is 69% of intake and almost exactly the 60 L/day the greenhouse needs after condensate
the loop that makes irrigation affordable: recovers about 85% of the 400 L/day (106 gal/day) the canopy transpires, the same closure BIOS-3 measured; without it irrigation is 400 L/day of real water
heat pump water heater, about 2 kWh/day for one person; at bare minimum this duty sits on the biomass stove instead
with a heat pump dryer, about 1 kWh/day and 11 L/day averaged
modern units use LESS water than hand washing, about 10 L (2.6 gal) per load, so it is close to water neutral against the kitchen sink

loops.name: Food
loops.demand: 2,600 kcal/day and about 75 g (2.6 oz) of protein, one moderately active adult, both tiers. CORRECTED FROM 2,200 kcal and 55 g: FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 puts a 70 kg adult male at physical activity level 1.75 at 2,900 kcal/day and a 57 kg adult female at 2,250, and homestead labour is not sedentary. Harvest must exceed intake by about 15 percent to cover the seed fraction and storage losses, so the real target is about 3,000 kcal/day of harvest. The diet that every area below is derived from: grain 1,200 kcal, pulse 700, greenhouse 550, fish 150. Luxury adds variety, spice, and serious preservation, not more calories.
loops.closure_note: The honest cap is light, and the light has to be measured, not asserted. Annual photosynthetically active radiation under glass at this site is about 20.2 mol/m2/day, but December is 6.7 mol/m2/day, below the 12 to 17 mol/m2/day leafy greens need and far below the 20 to 30 fruiting crops need: November to February the sun lit greenhouse holds, it does not produce, and four months of eating come out of the silo and the root cellar. Realised food energy for a well run unlit greenhouse here is about 7.2 kcal/m2/day (range 5 to 10), which is a canopy level light use efficiency of 0.20 g dry matter per mol of incident PAR, about 20 percent of the 1.0 g/mol a continuously closed optimal canopy manages, and that 20 percent realisation is what winter dead time, bed turnover, paths, and establishment gaps cost you. THE BIG CORRECTION, from the 2026-07-30 pass and still standing: a room is not a canopy. Counting the machines actually placed in data/machines/home_solo.ron gives 16 m2 of potato bed, 6 m2 of oilseed bed, 4 m2 of grain tray, about 18 m2 of tower canopy, and 2.6 m2 of tank, which is 46.6 m2 (502 sq ft) of lit canopy in a 1,156 m2 room, 4.0 percent of the floor. At 7.2 kcal/m2/day that is 335 kcal/day, not the catalogued 2,078 kcal/day; even crediting the full 116 m2 of lit floor the array spacing reserves it is 837 kcal/day. The indoor claim is over by 2.5x to 6.2x. NEW THIS PASS: the previous pass replaced that with an asserted 350 m2 of greenhouse canopy and never summed the loop, so nobody noticed that 350 m2 plus the two fields harvest 6,300 kcal/day against a 3,000 kcal/day requirement, more than double, while the nutrients loop assumed only about 1,900 kcal/day was exported. The greenhouse is now DERIVED from the diet instead: 550 kcal/day eaten becomes 633 kcal/day harvested becomes 88 m2 (950 sq ft) of bare canopy, and the design carries 200 m2 (2,150 sq ft) to buy crop failure resilience, succession gaps, the fact that the vegetable fraction is chosen for nutrition rather than calories, and the continuously closed canopy the air loop wants. The fields are grain 660 m2 and pulse 441 m2, and total harvest is 5,470 kcal/day against the 3,000 kcal/day requirement, so the loop closes and the deliberate surplus is 2,470 kcal/day, essentially all grain, which is exactly the trade surplus the nutrients loop then charges soil for. Arable including rotation is 1,700 to 2,100 m2 (0.17 to 0.21 ha, 0.42 to 0.52 acre), which lands on FAO's global arable per capita of about 0.19 ha, a good independent check. Protein closes with margin at about 103 g/day. Two open edges: fish feed, 83 to 110 kg/year that has to be grown on its own 30 to 110 m2 of lit water or bought, and the pulse crop itself, because dry bean at 2 t/ha is a continental figure and this maritime site wants an overwintered fava, which does not exist in data/plants.csv.
balance: Light cap: 3.9 kWh/m2/day x 3.6 MJ/kWh x 0.45 PAR fraction x 4.57 umol/J = 28.9 mol/m2/day outdoors; x 0.70 glazing = 20.2 mol/m2/day annual under glass. December: 1.3 kWh/m2/day gives 6.7 mol/m2/day under glass.

Realised yield, derivation now stated: 7.2 kcal/m2/day = 1.8 g edible dry matter/m2/day at 4 kcal/g, divided by harvest index 0.45 = 4.0 g total dry matter/m2/day, divided by 20.2 mol = 0.20 g dry matter per mol PAR, a 20% realisation of the 1.0 g/mol closed canopy figure. Biointensive at 700 to 1,000 m2 per person and 2,400 kcal/day is 2.4 to 3.4 kcal/m2/day, so this greenhouse is 2 to 3x biointensive, which is what glass and management buy.

Canopy as instantiated, CORRECTED: 8 potato beds x 2 m2 = 16, 3 oilseed x 2 = 6, 2 grain trays x 2 = 4, 9 towers x ~2 m2 leaf projected = 18, tank 1.6 x 1.6 = 2.6. Total 46.6 m2 in a 1,156 m2 room, not the 44 m2 previously stated.
Indoor supply as instantiated: 46.6 m2 x 7.2 = 335 kcal/day against the catalogued 2,078 kcal/day, over by 6.2x on canopy and 2.5x even crediting the full 116 m2 of lit floor (116 x 7.2 = 837).

Greenhouse area DERIVED, replacing the asserted 350 m2: diet 550 kcal/day from the greenhouse x 1.15 seed and storage = 633 kcal/day harvest, divided by 7.2 = 88 m2 bare. Carried at 200 m2 for crop failure, succession gaps, nutrition driven crop choice, and the air loop's continuous canopy. 200 x 7.2 = 1,440 kcal/day.

Grain field area: western Washington winter wheat at 4 to 6 t/ha = 0.5 kg/m2/year x 3,400 kcal/kg = 1,700 kcal/m2/year = 4.66 kcal/m2/day. Eating 1,200 kcal/day needs 1,380 kcal/day harvested = 296 m2; the design carries 660 m2 to bank a trade surplus, giving 3,076 kcal/day.

Pulse field area, CORRECTED: dry bean at 2 t/ha = 0.2 kg/m2/year x 3,330 kcal/kg = 666 kcal/m2/year = 1.82 kcal/m2/day. The previous pass sized 384 m2 against the 700 kcal/day EATEN; the harvest figure is 805 kcal/day, so the area is 441 m2.

TOTAL SUPPLY, the sum the previous pass never wrote: greenhouse 1,440 + grain 3,076 + pulse 804 + fish 150 = 5,470 kcal/day of harvest against a 3,000 kcal/day requirement. CLOSES. Deliberate surplus 2,470 kcal/day, of which 1,696 kcal/day (about 180 kg of wheat a year) actually leaves the farm and is charged to the nutrients loop.

Potato bed cross-check, CORRECTED AGAIN: the catalogued +120 kcal/day from 2.0 m2 is 60 kcal/m2/day = 21,900 kcal/m2/year = 28.4 kg/m2/year = 284 t/ha/year, against 50 t/ha per season for the best commercial field crop. The 2026-07-30 replacement of 45 to 60 kcal/day per bed is still 107 to 142 t/ha/year, which no sun lit greenhouse does. Honest: 2 cycles a year x 4 to 5 kg/m2/cycle x 770 kcal/kg over 2 m2 is 30 to 45 kcal/day per bed, point 38.

Potato plant-count cross-check against data/plants.csv: potato is 90 growth_days at 4 to 10 yield units, and data/food/crop_nutrition.ron is 150 g/unit, so one plant gives 600 to 1,500 g per cycle, mid 1,050 g = 11.7 g/day = 9 kcal/day. The catalogued 120 kcal/day therefore needs 13.3 plants in 2 m2, and at a conventional 4.4 plants/m2 a 2 m2 bed holds 9 plants and 2 cycles a year deliver 38 kcal/day. The bridge and the catalogue agree once the cycle count is honest.

Variety tower cross-check: the catalogued +92 kcal/day sits on 2.2 x 2.2 m of array spacing = 4.84 m2 of lit floor = 19 kcal/m2/day = 6,930 kcal/m2/year, which is 5.6x the top biointensive figure (the previous pass said 8x, which compares against the bottom of the range). Honest sun lit figure is 25 to 40 kcal/day per tower, point 35, and a good mixed vegetable canopy at 10 kg/m2/year and 300 kcal/kg is 8 kcal/m2/day, which brackets it.

YIELD BRIDGE FAILURE, new finding: data/plants.csv yield units multiplied by data/food/crop_nutrition.ron grams_per_yield_unit are dimensionally inconsistent across crop types, so most of this loop CANNOT be checked against the game data. Wheat: 8 to 20 units x 50 g = 400 to 1,000 g of grain per plant, against a real 1 to 3 g (5 t/ha at about 250 plants/m2 is 2 g), high by 200 to 500x. Sunflower: 50 to 200 units x 50 g = 2.5 to 10 kg of seed per plant against a real head of 50 to 150 g, high by 20 to 100x. Bean: 150 to 400 g/plant against 50 to 100 g, high by 2 to 4x. Lettuce: 600 to 1,200 g/head against 300 to 600 g, high by 2x. Potato at 600 to 1,500 g/plant is CORRECT, and crop_nutrition.ron's own header says only the potato bridge was ever calibrated. The grain and oilseed rows above are therefore grounded in FAO and extension yields per hectare, not in the game data.

loops.name: Air
loops.demand: 0.77 kg/day (1.7 lb/day) of oxygen consumed and 0.92 kg/day (2.0 lb/day) of carbon dioxide produced, at the 2,600 kcal/day metabolic rate above. CORRECTED FROM 0.55 kg/day, which was 29 percent below even the old 2,200 kcal figure and 35 percent below NASA's nominal. Plus trace contaminant control, which the old outline had in neither tier. On open Earth all of this is free ventilation. In a sealed habitat it is 5.8 kWh/day of machinery.
loops.closure_note: THIS LOOP CLOSES ON EARTH AND DOES NOT CLOSE SEALED AT THE BARE MINIMUM POWER TIER, which is a change of verdict from the previous pass and the honest reading of its own numbers. NASA's standard crew metabolic values are 0.84 kg of oxygen and 1.00 kg of carbon dioxide per crew member per day at 136.7 W (11,200 Btu/day, 2,822 kcal/day) and a respiratory quotient of 0.87. Reproducing that from first principles as a check: 11.81 MJ/day divided by 20.3 kJ per litre of oxygen is 582 L, which at 1.429 g/L is 0.83 kg, so the method agrees with NASA and can be scaled. At this homestead's 2,600 kcal/day it gives 0.77 kg of oxygen and 0.92 kg of carbon dioxide. Can the garden do it? NEW THIS PASS, and it is the reconciliation the previous pass missed: that pass sized the oxygen canopy at 36 m2 using a light use efficiency of 1.0 g dry matter per mol PAR while its own food loop implied 0.20 g/mol, a 5x internal contradiction inside one file. Doing it with the food loop's OWN realised yields instead: the 200 m2 greenhouse harvests 1,440 kcal/day of edible food, which is 343 g of edible dry matter, which at a harvest index of 0.45 is 762 g of total plant dry matter a day, which releases 813 g of oxygen against a 766 g requirement. The food area IS the air area, at 106 percent, and now that is demonstrated rather than asserted. BIOS-3 at Krasnoyarsk agrees from the other direction: 315 m3, 63 m2 of phytotron under xenon lamps, two to three crew, longest run 180 days, air regenerated to nearly 100 percent, water 85 to 95 percent, food only 50 to 80 percent, which is 21 to 32 m2 of INTENSELY LIT crop per person, the same 36 m2 the theoretical calculation gives when the canopy is closed and lit year round. TWO CATCHES, both of which the sealed case cannot escape. First, in a sealed volume net oxygen production equals the rate at which fixed carbon is REMOVED from the loop: composting the residue inside the envelope is slow combustion and gives back almost exactly the oxygen that growing it released, which is why BIOS-3 dried and stored its inedible biomass or oxidised it outside the loop. Second, December: at 6.7 mol/m2/day the canopy is below the compensation point and is a net oxygen CONSUMER for about four months, and oxygen is not practically storable at homestead scale. So a sealed habitat needs the machine, and the machine is what breaks the tier: 5.0 kWh/day for electrolytic oxygen (1 kg of oxygen carries 0.125 kg of hydrogen and real electrolysers use 50 to 55 kWh per kg of hydrogen, so 6.5 kWh per kg of oxygen; ISS flight hardware runs about 2 kW for six crew, which is 8 kWh/day per person), 0.6 kWh/day for a regenerable carbon dioxide sorbent bed, and 0.2 kWh/day for trace contaminant control. That 5.8 kWh/day is 145 percent of the ENTIRE 4.0 kWh/day bare minimum power budget, so the sealed bare minimum is really 9.8 kWh/day and 24 panels, not 4.0 and 11. The bioregenerative alternative is worse: 720 mol of PAR a day from LEDs at 2.9 umol/J is 69 kWh/day, 17 times the bare minimum budget, so electrolysis beats photosynthesis by about 12x on electricity, which is exactly why the ISS uses a machine and not a garden.
balance: Metabolic: 2,600 kcal/day = 10,879 kJ / 20.3 kJ per L O2 = 536 L O2/day x 1.429 g/L = 0.766 kg O2/day. CO2 at RQ 0.87 = 466 L x 1.977 g/L = 0.922 kg/day.
Method check against NASA: at 136.7 W (2,822 kcal/day) the same formula gives 0.83 kg O2/day against NASA's stated 0.84, and 1.00 kg CO2/day matching NASA exactly.
Pre-audit figure: 0.55 kg/day is 29% below the 0.65 kg/day that 2,200 kcal/day implies and 35% below NASA's 0.84 nominal.

Canopy needed, theoretical: 0.766 kg O2 needs 1.05 kg CO2 fixed = 0.287 kg C = 0.72 kg dry biomass; at 1.0 g/mol PAR that is 720 mol/day; at 20.2 mol/m2/day annual under glass = 36 m2; at 6.7 mol/m2/day December = 107 m2, and below compensation the canopy is net negative regardless of area.

Canopy needed, REALISED, using the food loop's own numbers: the 200 m2 greenhouse harvests 1,440 kcal/day = 343 g edible dry matter / 0.45 harvest index = 762 g total dry matter/day = 25.4 mol CH2O = 813 g O2/day and 1,118 g CO2 fixed. Against 766 g O2 needed and 922 g CO2 produced that is 106% and 121%. The two loops now agree; the previous pass had 36 m2 from a 1.0 g/mol assumption sitting beside a food loop implying 0.20 g/mol, a 5x contradiction.
BIOS-3 anchor: 63 m2 of lit phytotron per 2 to 3 crew = 21 to 32 m2/person for near total air regeneration under lamps. Agrees with the 36 m2 theoretical figure.

Composting penalty: the 762 g/day of dry matter splits into 343 g eaten and respired and 419 g of residue; composting that residue inside a sealed envelope oxidises the same carbon the canopy fixed, so a sealed home that grows and composts inside nets close to ZERO oxygen. Export the carbon (silo, biochar, airlock) or there is no oxygen.
December: 6.7 mol/m2/day is below the compensation point, so the canopy is a net O2 consumer for about four months and no area fixes it.
Electrolytic O2: 0.766 kg O2 x 0.125 kg H2 per kg O2 = 0.096 kg H2 x 52 kWh/kg = 5.0 kWh/day. ISS OGA flight hardware: about 2 kW for 6 crew = 8 kWh/day per person.
CO2 removal: regenerable sorbent bed, ISS CDRA magnitude, 0.5 to 1.0 kWh/day per person. Point 0.6.

Trace contaminants: NASA TCCS is an activated charcoal bed plus a 400 C catalytic oxidiser plus a lithium hydroxide post sorbent at about 200 W = 0.2 kWh/day. HEPA is particulate only and removes none of it.

SEALED TOTAL: 5.0 + 0.6 + 0.2 = 5.8 kWh/day against a 4.0 kWh/day bare minimum budget = 145%. DOES NOT CLOSE at this tier. The sealed bare minimum is 9.8 kWh/day, needing 24 panels and 8 banks instead of 11 and 3.

Bioregenerative alternative under LEDs: 720 mol/day / 2.9 umol/J = 248 MJ = 69 kWh/day, assuming the optimal 1.0 g/mol; at the realised 0.20 g/mol it is 345 kWh/day. Electrolysis is 12x cheaper at best and 60x cheaper at realistic garden efficiency.
OPEN EARTH: none of the above binds. Ventilation is free, the atmosphere is the buffer, and the loop closes trivially. Everything in this loop that fails, fails only inside a sealed hull.

Energy equivalent of oxygen 20.3 kJ per litre at a mixed diet respiratory quotient.

Electrolyser 50 to 55 kWh per kg of hydrogen; horticultural LED efficacy 2.8 to 3.0 umol/J.
Plant dry matter treated as CH2O at 30 g/mol, so 1 mol of fixed carbon releases 1 mol (32 g) of O2 and consumes 1 mol (44 g) of CO2.

loops.name: Climate (heating and cooling)
loops.demand: Hold 20 C (68 F) year round against 2,610 heating degree days base 18.3 C and 44 cooling degree days. For the 320 m2 (3,444 sq ft) house of the luxury tier the fabric plus ventilation heat loss coefficient is 182 W/K, so the NET annual heat demand is about 9,800 kWh/year (31 kWh/m2/year net, 42 gross), about 63 kWh/day gross on a January day and 50 kWh/day net of gains. For the 40 m2 (430 sq ft) bare minimum dwelling the same shell quality gives about 30 W/K and only about 650 kWh/year, because one occupant plus 4 kWh/day of appliances very nearly heats it. Cooling is a non-need at this site.
loops.closure_note: Insulation is the real machine and the shell numbers were never written down before this audit, so here they are: 320 m2 of floor and 320 m2 of roof, 216 m2 of wall of which 32 m2 is glazing, at U values of 0.15 for walls, 0.10 for roof, 0.15 for floor, and 0.80 for triple glazing, gives a fabric loss of 133 W/K; 960 m3 at 0.35 air changes per hour through an 85 percent heat recovery ventilator plus 0.1 air changes of infiltration adds 49 W/K; total 182 W/K. Internal gains are real: the occupant is a steady 100 W (2.4 kWh/day), all 4.0 kWh/day of bare minimum electricity lands indoors as heat, and 16 m2 of south glazing at 0.8 kWh/m2/day and a solar heat gain coefficient of 0.5 adds 6.4 kWh/day in December, about 12.8 kWh/day in total. CORRECTED THIS PASS, and it is a method error not an arithmetic one: the previous pass computed 11,400 kWh/year from 182 W/K times 2,610 heating degree days base 18.3 C, then subtracted the internal gains again to get 8,800 kWh net. Degree days at base 18.3 C ALREADY credit about 1.7 K of free gains, which is precisely why the base sits below a 20 C setpoint, so that subtracts them twice. Redone by the balance point method, 12.8 kWh/day of gains against 182 W/K covers 2.9 K, so the balance point is 17.1 C, the degree days at that base are about 2,235, and the net heat is 9,800 kWh/year, 11 percent higher than published. The 40 m2 tier was also wrong: 40 W/K was asserted, and deriving it from the same U values gives about 30 W/K, whereupon the same 8 kWh/day of gains covers 11 K, the balance point falls to 8.9 C, and the net heat is about 650 kWh/year or 16 kWh/m2/year, which lands on the Passive House criterion of 15. That makes the tier jump far bigger than stated: 8x the floor area is 15x the heat and 15x the firewood, and it is the largest single lever in this entire outline. Bare minimum closes on the woodlot: 9,800 kWh of net heat at 70 percent stove efficiency is 50.4 GJ of wood, which is 2.4 cords or 5.9 m3 (208 cu ft) of solid wood a year, which at a managed Pacific Northwest growth of 5 to 10 m3 per hectare per year (about one cord per acre per year, the usual rule of thumb) is 0.59 to 1.18 ha (1.5 to 2.9 acres) of woodlot. The 40 m2 dwelling needs 0.4 m3, a fifth of a cord, off 0.04 to 0.08 ha. The luxury heat pump does NOT close in December: 41 kWh/day of thermal at a seasonal coefficient of performance of 3.0 is 13.7 kWh/day electrical, and a December day at 50 kWh/day thermal and a real air source coefficient of 2.5 at 5 C is 20.0 kWh/day electrical, on top of an 11.0 kWh/day base load, against a 28 panel array making 11.6 kWh/day that month. The correction a real off grid builder makes is the one adopted here: deep winter stays on biomass and the heat pump does shoulder seasons and summer cooling, where 12 kWh/day of thermal at a coefficient of 4.0 is 3 kWh/day electrical and about 5 kWh/day averaged over the year. In the sealed mothership case the problem inverts entirely: there is no heating load and the question becomes heat rejection, where one occupant plus 16 kWh/day of equipment is 767 W needing about 4 m2 of radiator, while the 200 m2 glass roofed growing bay in full sun absorbs about 200 kW and needs on the order of 1,000 m2 of radiator, 250 times the house's own.
balance: Ventilation: 960 m3 x 0.35 ACH = 336 m3/h = 112 W/K, x 0.15 after an 85% HRV = 16.8 W/K; plus 0.1 ACH infiltration = 32 W/K. Total 49 W/K. Cross-check: ASHRAE 62.2 for 3,444 sq ft and one bedroom asks 200 m3/h (0.21 ACH), which would give 42 W/K and a total of 175 W/K, so the 182 used here is 4% conservative.
Total heat loss coefficient 182 W/K.

Balance point, CORRECTED METHOD: gains 12.8 kWh/day = 533 W, divided by 182 W/K = 2.9 K, so the balance point is 20 - 2.9 = 17.1 C. Degree days at base 17.1 C are about 2,235 (2,610 x 0.856, the ratio from a monthly mean recomputation of the Bremerton normals).

Net annual heat: 182 W/K x 2,235 C-days x 24 h = 9,760 kWh/year, call it 9,800, which is 31 kWh/m2/year net and 42 gross (Passive House is 15, a typical new US home is 100 to 150). The previous pass published 8,800 kWh/year by subtracting gains that base 18.3 C degree days had already credited.

January: mean outdoor 5.5 C, delta T 14.5 K, 182 x 14.5 = 2,639 W = 63 kWh/day gross; minus 12.8 kWh/day of gains = 50 kWh/day net. The previous pass's demand line said 61 and 48, which disagreed with its own balance line; 63 and 50 is correct.
Heating season (240 days): 9,800 / 240 = 41 kWh/day net average.

Wood: 9,800 kWh = 35.3 GJ delivered / 0.70 stove efficiency = 50.4 GJ of wood / 20.7 GJ per cord = 2.4 cords = 5.9 m3 (208 cu ft) solid/year; at 5 to 10 m3/ha/year growth that is 0.59 to 1.18 ha (1.5 to 2.9 acres) of woodlot.

Bare minimum 40 m2 dwelling, CORRECTED: fabric 55 m2 opaque wall x 0.15 + 40 roof x 0.10 + 40 floor x 0.15 + 8 glazing x 0.80 = 24.7 W/K, plus 4.9 W/K of ventilation (30 m3/h for one person after HRV, plus 0.1 ACH of 100 m3) = about 30 W/K, not the 40 asserted. Gains 8.0 kWh/day = 333 W cover 11.1 K, so the balance point is 8.9 C, degree days at that base are about 900, and net heat is 30 x 900 x 24 = 650 kWh/year = 16 kWh/m2/year, right on the Passive House criterion. Wood: 650 kWh = 2.3 GJ / 0.70 = 3.3 GJ = 0.16 cords = 0.4 m3/year off 0.04 to 0.08 ha.

TIER LEVER: 8x the floor area (40 to 320 m2) is 6x the heat loss coefficient (30 to 182 W/K) and 15x the heat and firewood (650 to 9,800 kWh/year, 0.4 to 5.9 m3). Nothing else in this outline moves a number that hard.

Luxury heat pump: 41 kWh/day thermal / COP 3.0 = 13.7 kWh/day electrical seasonal; 50 / 2.5 = 20.0 kWh/day in December, on top of an 11.0 kWh/day base load, against 11.6 kWh/day from a 28 panel array. DOES NOT CLOSE in December; see the power loop's 78 panel figure for what it would take.

Heat pump on its real duty (shoulder season and cooling only): 12 kWh/day thermal / COP 4.0 = 3 kWh/day electrical, about 5 kWh/day averaged over the year. The catalogued number was right for this duty and wrong for full winter heating.
Cooling: 44 C cooling degree days. Shading, night ventilation, and thermal mass carry it; the spot air conditioner is a heat wave machine, not a season.

Sealed case: 100 W occupant + 667 W equipment = 767 W to reject; a 300 K radiator at emissivity 0.9 and a 50% view factor emits about 200 W/m2 net, so about 4 m2. CORRECTED: the sunlit growing bay is this design's 200 m2 greenhouse, about 200 kW absorbed and about 1,000 m2 of radiator, 250x the house. The previous pass used a 4,895 m2 area that appears nowhere in this design.

Seasoned Douglas fir at about 20.7 GJ per cord and 2.4 m3 of solid wood per cord, wood stove efficiency 0.70, managed Pacific Northwest woodlot growth 5 to 10 m3 per hectare per year, which is the familiar one cord per acre per year rule of thumb.

loops.name: Nutrients and waste
loops.demand: About 6.0 kg/day (13 lb/day) of wet organic material back to the soil: 1.5 kg of human excreta, 0.2 kg of kitchen scraps, and 4.3 kg of wet crop residue. CORRECTED TWICE, from 1.5 kg/day (excreta only, while the text said food scraps, crop residue, and humanure) and then from 4.3 kg/day, which counted the residue of a farm feeding one person rather than the residue of the farm this design actually draws. In nutrient terms the crops take up about 15.4 kg of nitrogen, 2.6 kg of phosphorus, and 20.5 kg of potassium a year, roughly double the previously published figures for the same reason.
loops.closure_note: THIS LOOP DOES NOT CLOSE, and saying so is the point, but the previous pass got the shape of the failure wrong. Its numbers (nitrogen 75 percent returned, phosphorus 90, potassium 66, with potassium called the tightest) came from counting only the food the resident EATS, 527 kg of plant dry matter a year, when the farm that feeds them actually grows 1,027 kg because the grain field is deliberately oversized for trade. Redone against real production: uptake is 15.4 kg N, 2.6 kg P, and 20.5 kg K a year. Splitting that between edible and residue instead of averaging one figure across both changes the answer, because residue is where nearly all the potassium sits and residue is composted straight back. Returns are 8.1 kg N (53 percent), 1.93 kg P (75 percent), and 19.1 kg K (93 percent). So potassium is the LEAST tight, not the tightest, and nitrogen is the biggest raw gap at 7.3 kg a year, three and a half times what was published. Nitrogen nonetheless CLOSES, and the reason was already sitting in this outline uncredited: the 441 m2 pulse field fixes about 4.4 kg a year and the 560 to 960 m2 of rotation and green manure land fixes another 5.6 to 9.6, so 10 to 14 kg against a 7.3 kg gap. That is what the rotation land is FOR, and the previous pass listed it without ever putting it in the balance. Potassium is short 1.4 kg a year on the compost balance, and in 1,400 mm of annual rain soil leaching takes another 10 to 20 percent of the pool, so call the real gap 4.5 kg; wood ash returns 1.4 kg of it and the rest is traded in as potash. Phosphorus is the one that can never be closed in principle, because there is no biological phosphorus fixation: nothing on the homestead makes phosphorus, so every gram that leaves is bought back from a mine. And export is the term that decides everything. This design harvests 5,470 kcal/day against a 3,000 kcal/day requirement and genuinely ships about 180 kg of wheat a year off the farm, carrying 3.8 kg of nitrogen, 0.63 kg of phosphorus, and 0.81 kg of potassium. That single flow is larger than everything the resident's own body returns. Trading calories is trading soil. Over 25 years at that rate the homestead ships out about 16 kg of phosphorus, roughly 110 kg of rock phosphate to buy back. One more honesty note: the wood ash that closes part of the potassium gap is not an input at all, it is phosphorus and potassium mined out of the woodlot's own soil and moved to the garden, so the woodlot pays for it. None of this closes a cannot close loop; it puts a number on why raw chemistry is on that list.
balance: Farm production, the term the previous pass omitted: plant harvest is 1,440 (greenhouse) + 3,076 (grain) + 804 (pulse) = 5,320 kcal/day = 462 kg/year of edible dry matter at 4.2 kcal/g; at harvest index 0.45 total plant dry matter is 1,027 kg/year, of which 565 kg is residue.
Uptake at N 1.5%, P 0.25%, K 2.0% of dry matter: N 15.4, P 2.58, K 20.5 kg/year. The previous pass published 7.9 / 1.3 / 10.5 by counting only the 527 kg the resident eats.

Split check: edible 462 kg at N 2.1 / P 0.35 / K 0.45% = N 9.7, P 1.62, K 2.08; residue 565 kg at N 1.0 / P 0.17 / K 3.25% = N 5.7, P 0.96, K 18.4. Sums match the whole plant uptake, which is the point: potassium lives in the residue.
Return 1, residue composted (all of it stays on the farm): N 5.7 x 0.70 = 4.0; P 0.96 x 0.90 = 0.86; K 18.4 x 0.90 = 16.6.

Return 2, excreta: the resident eats 2,450 kcal/day of plant food = 213 kg/year of dry matter carrying N 4.5, P 0.75, K 0.96; after composting losses N 3.1, P 0.67, K 0.86. Cross-check against the source separation literature, which gives 2.5 to 4.3 kg N, 0.4 to 1.0 kg P, 0.9 to 1.4 kg K per person year: agrees.
Return 3, seed and storage loss fraction (15% of edible = 69 kg/year, resown or composted): N 1.0, P 0.22, K 0.28 after losses.

Return 4, wood ash from 2.4 cords (about 2,800 kg of wood at 1.0% ash = 28 kg): at 6% K2O and 1.5% P2O5 that is 1.4 kg K and 0.18 kg P. NOT a new input: it is mined from the woodlot's own soil and moved to the garden.
NET RETURNED: N 8.1, P 1.93, K 19.1 kg/year. Against uptake: N 53%, P 75%, K 93%. Previously published: 75%, 90%, 66% (and before the first audit, an unreproducible 587% / 533% / 197%).

Nitrogen gap 7.3 kg/year, and it CLOSES: the 441 m2 pulse field at 100 kg N/ha/year fixes 4.4 kg and the 560 to 960 m2 of rotation and green manure fixes 5.6 to 9.6 kg, so 10.0 to 14.0 kg against a 7.3 kg gap. The previous pass asked for 200 m2 of dedicated legume against a 2.0 kg gap and never credited the rotation land it had already listed.

Potassium gap 1.4 kg/year on the compost balance; add soil leaching at 10 to 20% of the pool in 1,400 mm of rain (about 3.1 kg/year) and the real gap is 4.5 kg. Wood ash covers 1.4. Residual about 3.1 kg/year traded in as mineral potash.

Phosphorus gap 0.65 kg/year, of which 0.63 is the exported grain and the remainder is leaching. There is no biological phosphorus fixation at all, so this deficit is permanent rather than recoverable. Over 25 years: about 16 kg of P, roughly 110 kg of rock phosphate.

Export term: 462 kg edible harvested minus 213 eaten minus 69 seed and storage = 180 kg/year of grain leaving = 493 g/day = 1,676 kcal/day. At N 2.1%, P 0.35%, K 0.40% that is N 3.8, P 0.63, K 0.81 kg/year off the farm, which is more nitrogen and phosphorus than the resident's own body returns.

Compost mass check: 6.0 kg/day of wet feedstock (1.5 excreta + 0.2 kitchen + 4.3 wet residue) losing 60 to 70% to water and carbon dioxide gives 1.8 to 2.4 kg/day of finished compost. The two catalogued composters at 0.6 kg/day each deliver 1.2 kg/day, about half the residue stream. Nutrient in 1.2 kg of compost at 1.5% N, 0.5% P, 1.0% K is 18 g N, 6 g P, 12 g K a day, so the catalogued figure is right as COMPOST and wrong by about 70x if read as NUTRIENT.

Wet residue derivation: grain straw 330 kg dry at 12% moisture = 375 kg wet; pulse haulm 150 kg dry = 176 kg wet; greenhouse residue 153 kg dry at 85% moisture = 1,020 kg wet. Total about 1,570 kg/year = 4.3 kg/day wet.
assumptions: Excreta nutrient figures from the source separation literature (Vinneras and Jonsson 2002; Jonsson et al. 2004, EcoSanRes Guidelines on the Use of Urine and Faeces in Crop Production), used here as a CROSS-CHECK on a figure derived from what the resident actually eats.

Whole plant nutrient contents N 1.5%, P 0.25%, K 2.0% of dry matter, split as edible N 2.1 / P 0.35 / K 0.45% and residue N 1.0 / P 0.17 / K 3.25%. The split is what the previous pass lacked, and it is why its potassium verdict inverted.
Composting losses: N minus 30% (range 20 to 40, as ammonia), P and K minus 10% (range 5 to 15, leaching). Urine diversion is what keeps the nitrogen loss at the low end.
Biological nitrogen fixation 50 to 150 kg per hectare per year for a well managed legume or green manure crop; point estimate 100.
Wood ash 0.5 to 1.5% of wood mass at 3 to 9% K2O and 1 to 2% P2O5; point estimate 1.0%, 6%, and 1.5%.
Soil potassium leaching 10 to 20% of the exchangeable pool per year in a 1,400 mm rainfall maritime climate.
The balance is stated with and without the traded grain surplus, because export is what flips the sign.

loops.closure_note: The house is the container that makes every other loop's numbers work, and it had no numbers of its own until this audit. The bare minimum floor area is grounded in the UK Nationally Described Space Standard, which sets 39 m2 for a one bedroom one person dwelling, and for the sealed case in NASA's net habitable volume guidance, which puts the long duration lower limit near 25 m3 per person while the ISS actually provides about 65 m3 of habitable volume per crew member at a crew of six (the previous pass said 100, which is the pressurised rather than the habitable figure). BIOS-3 ran 315 m3 for one to three crew. The 8x jump between the two tiers, 40 m2 against 320 m2, is the single largest lever in the whole outline, and the corrected climate arithmetic makes it larger than published: it is the difference between 0.4 m3 and 5.9 m3 of firewood a year and between 0.04 ha and 1.18 ha of woodlot, a 15x swing on the strength of a floor plan. Nothing else in this document moves a number that hard. The land total is worth sitting with: the arable line of 0.17 to 0.21 ha lands on FAO's global arable per capita of about 0.19 ha, which is a reassuring independent check, and the woodlot is what makes the total large, so it is also the term that disappears the moment you stop heating with wood, or the moment you build the small house. The workshop is what keeps every other machine alive, and at the luxury tier it also makes things: printed spare parts, custom brackets, repaired boards. What it cannot make is the panel's cells, the battery's cells, the pump's windings, or any circuit board, which is the equipment replacement entry in the panel below and is unchanged by this audit.

scaling.note: Get one resident exactly right first, then most of this is arithmetic. These are the terms that do NOT scale linearly, which is why the solo design has to be correct before anyone multiplies it.
scales_linearly: Food area: kcal, protein, greenhouse canopy, grain and pulse field, rotation land. N residents is N times the area, with a small saving because a bigger field wastes less edge.
Water: household litres, greywater recovery, evapotranspiration off the (larger) canopy.
Nutrients: uptake, excreta return, residue return, the phosphorus deficit. The P gap per person is unchanged, so N people ship out N times the phosphorus.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide: per person metabolic rates are per person.
Electrolytic life support in the sealed case: 5.8 kWh/day per person, because it is a chemical duty, not an overhead.
does_not_scale_linearly: AIR VOLUME. Habitable volume per person falls with crew size because circulation, galley, and hygiene spaces are shared: NASA's 25 m3/person floor is for the FIRST person and a crew of four does not need 100 m3 of net habitable volume per head. Do not multiply the 960 m3 house by N.

THERMAL MASS AND HEAT LOSS. Heat loss scales with envelope AREA, and area goes as volume to the two thirds. Doubling the occupancy of one building barely changes the heating bill, while building a second building nearly doubles it. Worse, occupants are 100 W heaters each: 4 people in the 320 m2 house add 300 W of gains, lift the balance point by 1.6 K, and cut the heating bill by about 12 percent before anything else changes.

PEAK POWER. Peak is not energy. Four people do not run four ovens at once, so peak grows roughly as the square root of crew size, but the battery bus must still carry the worst simultaneous minute. Size energy per person and peak per household.

SOLAR ARRAY IN DECEMBER. Energy is linear but ROOF is not: 11 panels per person at 2 m2 each is 22 m2, so four people want 88 m2 of December-optimal south roof on a 320 m2 house. The array outgrows the roof before it outgrows the budget.

THE WOODLOT. Firewood tracks the building, not the crew: four people in one 320 m2 house burn the same 5.9 m3 as one person in it, so per person woodlot area falls by 4x. Sharing a roof is the single largest land saving of adding a resident.

MACHINE COUNT. Machines come in integer sizes with minimum viable ones. One well pump, one purifier, one cistern, one composter bay, and one workshop serve several people; the second person costs almost no capital and the fifth costs a whole second machine.

STORAGE AUTONOMY. A shared cistern and a shared battery bank get RELATIVELY smaller per person for the same days of autonomy only if demand is well correlated; if it is not, the buffer must cover the peak day, not the average.

cannot_close.note: Five loops stay open no matter how good the homestead is: electronics and semiconductors, metal from raw ore, medicine synthesis, equipment replacement, and raw chemistry inputs. This audit did not close any of them and made one of them sharper: the nutrients loop above puts a real number on the phosphorus gap, which is the raw chemistry entry. The gap is not a failure; it is why neighbors, trade, and civilization exist.

footer: Five of these seven loops close. Nutrients does not, because nothing on a homestead makes phosphorus and every calorie traded away is soil traded away. Air does not either, but only inside a sealed hull, where regenerating one person's oxygen costs 5.8 kWh/day against a 4.0 kWh/day home: on open Earth that loop is free. A single person can close energy, water, climate, and food at a named place with stated assumptions, in a 40 m2 dwelling that is nearly self heating or a 320 m2 house that burns two and a half cords a year to be comfortable.
